Received 28 November 2024 l Revised 12 February 2025 l Accepted 17 February 2025 l Published online 11 June 2025 Abstract: Objective: Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality in women globally, with invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) as the predominant subtype. Regional lymph node (LN) metastasis significantly impacts prognosis, staging, and treatment strategies. However, the role of deep learning in predicting LN metastasis is underexplored. To develop and evaluate a deep learning model leveraging clinicopathological features for predicting LN metastasis in IDC patients, with an aim to enhance diagnostic accuracy and reduce reliance on invasive methods. Material and Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted on 351 IDC cases from a tertiary-care hospital. Input variables included clinicopathological features: age, tumor size, modified Bloom-Richardson grade, ER, PR, HER2 receptor status, Ki-67 index, and microvessel density (MVD). LN status was dichotomized using a cut-off ratio of 0.3. A neural network model with an input layer of 8 neurons, 3 hidden layers (50 neurons each), and ReLU activation was developed. Data were split into training (70%) and test (30%) sets. Predictive accuracy was evaluated using standard performance metrics. Results: The mean age was 46.4±11.29 years and tumor volume averaged 44.9 cm³. Low ER (35.6%) and PR (26.8%) positivity rates were observed, with HER2 positivity at 21.7%. The model achieved 78.3% accuracy in predicting LN metastasis. The F1 score of the model was 0.83. JSON: Name: deep_clinicopath_ln_prediction Title: Deep neural network prediction of regional lymph node metastasis in invasive ductal breast carcinoma using clinicopathological features Short Hypothesis: A deep neural network trained on clinicopathological features (age, tumor volume, Bloom–Richardson grade, ER, PR, HER2, Ki-67, microvessel density) will predict regional lymph node metastasis defined by lymph node ratio ≥0.3 with higher area under the ROC curve than a logistic regression model trained on the same features. Related Work: Prior work has applied statistical and machine learning methods to predict lymph node metastasis from clinicopathological data or imaging. Conventional approaches use logistic regression or simple tree-based models on clinicopathological variables and report moderate discrimination but limited sensitivity for clinically relevant subgroups. Gradient boosting and TabNet have shown improved performance on structured features but can overfit on single-center cohorts and are sensitive to feature selection. Deep learning applied to medical images (ultrasound, CT, MRI, DCE-MRI, and whole-slide histopathology) achieves higher AUCs when image content is available; however, image-based models require large, standardized imaging datasets and are less applicable where only pathology reports are available. Multimodal models combining clinicopathological variables and imaging or multi-omics improve accuracy but require complex data fusion and are less validated externally. Common limitations across studies include single-center data, small sample sizes for subgroups, lack of external validation, arbitrary label thresholds, limited model calibration reporting, and reduced interpretability of complex models. Abstract: Predicting regional lymph node metastasis in invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) using routinely collected clinicopathological features can reduce dependence on invasive staging procedures. We propose developing and evaluating a feedforward deep neural network that maps eight clinicopathological inputs (age, tumor volume, Bloom–Richardson grade, ER, PR, HER2, Ki-67, microvessel density) to a binary outcome defined by lymph node ratio ≥0.3. The primary contribution is a rigorous, reproducible experimental pipeline comparing the deep neural network to standard baselines (logistic regression, gradient boosting, TabNet) and to ablated feature sets, with model selection via nested cross-validation and external validation on an independent cohort. Evaluation will report discrimination, calibration, class-specific sensitivity and specificity, and clinical utility metrics. Expected outcomes are whether a neural network provides statistically and clinically meaningful improvement in AUC and decision-support performance over classical models when only clinicopathological data are available, and characterization of which feature groups drive performance. The work aims to quantify model benefit and limitations for potential clinical integration. Experiments: Datasets: primary dataset: 351 consecutive IDC-NOS cases with eight clinicopathological features and LNR label (≥0.3) from the tertiary hospital; external validation dataset: at least one independent multicenter cohort ≥500 cases with identical feature set or harmonized mapping; optional augmentation: subset with paired imaging or WSIs if available. Data splits: primary dataset: stratified 70% train / 30% internal test; within training perform 5-fold cross-validation and nested hyperparameter tuning; external validation withheld until final model selection. Baselines: (1) logistic regression with L2 penalty and standardized features; (2) random forest; (3) gradient boosting machine (e.g., XGBoost/LightGBM); (4) TabNet; (5) simple multilayer perceptron (MLP) with one hidden layer. Proposed model: MLP with 8-input neurons and 3 hidden layers (50 neurons each) using ReLU; train with Adam optimizer, learning rate grid search. Preprocessing: continuous features standardized; categorical features one-hot or ordinal as appropriate; missing data imputed with median for continuous and mode for categorical. Class imbalance: report raw and class-weighted training; evaluate both. Hyperparameter tuning: nested CV grid or Bayesian optimization for learning rate, weight decay, layer sizes, dropout. Evaluation metrics: primary metric AUC-ROC; secondary metrics accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1-score, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, calibration (Brier score, calibration curve), decision curve analysis, and net benefit at clinically relevant thresholds. Statistical tests: Delong test for AUC differences between models; 95% confidence intervals via bootstrapping (1000 resamples). Ablation studies: (A) feature-group ablation: remove (i) receptor markers (ER/PR/HER2), (ii) proliferation/angiogenesis (Ki-67/MVD), (iii) tumor morphology (volume/BR), (B) architecture ablation: vary depth/width and activation functions, (C) label threshold sensitivity: repeat experiments with LNR cutoffs 0.2 and 0.4. Additional comparisons: train models using only clinicopathological features versus clinicopathological + imaging (if available) to quantify multimodal lift. Report computation: training epochs, early stopping, total parameters, GPU/CPU used. Risk Factors and Limitations: Limited sample size and single-center provenance of the primary dataset may cause overfitting and reduce external generalizability; external validation cohorts may not share identical measurement protocols for tumor volume, Ki-67, or MVD, causing distribution shift. The binary label based on LNR ≥0.3 is an arbitrary threshold that may not reflect clinical heterogeneity and may introduce label noise. Class imbalance (fewer LNR ≥0.3 cases) will reduce sensitivity and inflate apparent specificity. Clinicopathological measurements (ER/PR/HER2 scoring, Ki-67, MVD) have inter-observer variability that injects noise into inputs. Model interpretability is limited for deep networks, complicating clinical acceptance. Performance gains vs. classical models may be marginal and not clinically meaningful. Computationally, deeper or multimodal models require greater resources for hyperparameter tuning and external validation. Regulatory, legal, and deployment constraints and lack of prospective clinical outcome data limit immediate clinical translation.
